title: Signature Four-Note Quarter Tune
body:
Specifications

An original Signature quarter tune played on four rods tuned to C, E, G, and A, with permutations invented for this design and labelled signature-original. The tune is not Westminster, Whittington, or any historical chime, and it is never presented as one. Its first quarter plays C, G, E, A, and the later quarters build on that phrase.

Mechanism

The tune uses four permutations of its four notes: C, G, E, A at the first quarter; G, E, A, C and A, C, G, E at the half hour; E, A, C, G, A, G, E, C, and C, G, E, A at the third quarter; and the full set at the hour, followed by the hour strikes. Each phrase is played as three quarter notes and a dotted half note, in the same rhythm as a traditional quarter chime, so the tune sounds familiar in shape while being original in notes.

Maintenance

Keep the four rods clean, check the hammer alignment, and test the full hour after any service, because a Signature tune's faults show at the hour, where the full sequence plays. Never retune a rod without recording the new tuning, because the tune depends on it.

Build and restoration guidance

When setting the Signature barrel, verify the first quarter's phrase before the longer quarters, and confirm the hour strike follows the full sequence. Record the tune's permutations in the service notes so the next service can check them.

Tools

Chime rod gauges, hammer tool, screwdrivers, and a tune chart.

title: Signature Eight-Note Descending Tune
body:
Specifications

An original Signature eight-rod tune that descends the scale at the first quarter and builds through the hour, invented for this design and labelled signature-original. It shares the eight-rod structure of the historical eight-bell chimes but uses its own melodic shape, and it is never presented as Whittington or St Michael.

Mechanism

The first quarter plays eight notes descending from the shortest rod to the longest, the half hour plays sixteen, the third quarter twenty-four, and the full hour thirty-two, followed by the hour strikes. The descending first quarter is the tune's signature, and the later quarters vary the descent rather than repeating it exactly, so the tune stays recognisable without becoming monotonous.

Maintenance

Keep all eight rods clean and check the hammers in order, because one dead hammer breaks the descent and is obvious at the first quarter. Check the selector so the movement is fully on the Signature tune before testing.

Build and restoration guidance

When setting the Signature barrel, verify the eight-note descent first, then the longer quarters, because the barrel is pinned as a single sequence used twice per hour. Record the rod order in the service notes.

Tools

Chime rod gauges, hammer tool, screwdrivers, and a scale reference.

title: Signature Rising Morning Tune
body:
Specifications

An original Signature tune that rises rather than falls, made for a morning chime option that sounds bright at the start of the day. It is played on eight rods, its first quarter rises from the lowest rod to the highest, and it is labelled signature-original throughout.

Mechanism

The first quarter plays eight notes rising from the longest rod to the shortest, the half hour plays sixteen, the third quarter twenty-four, and the full hour thirty-two, followed by the hour strikes. The rising shape gives the tune a lifting character, and the later quarters build on the rise with variations, so the full hour sounds like a completed phrase rather than a repeated scale.

Maintenance

Keep the eight rods clean, check the hammers from longest to shortest, and test the full hour after any service. A rising tune that sounds flat at the start usually has a hammer striking the longest rod off-centre.

Build and restoration guidance

When setting the barrel, verify the rising first quarter before the longer quarters, and confirm the hour strike follows the full sequence. Record the rod order and the tune's shape in the service notes.

Tools

Chime rod gauges, hammer tool, screwdrivers, and a scale reference.

title: Signature Triple-Chime Selection Tune
body:
Specifications

An original Signature third option for a triple-chime clock, alongside the Signature four-note tune and the Signature eight-note tune, so the owner can choose between three Signature tunes without any historical chime. It is played on the same multi-rod set as the other two, and it is labelled signature-original.

Mechanism

The tune accumulates through the hour like the other quarter chimes, with a short sequence at the first quarter and the full sequence at the hour, followed by the hour strikes. The selector moves the hammers or the barrel to the Signature third track, and the tune's shape is distinct from both the four-note and the eight-note Signature tunes, so the choice is audible at the first quarter.

Maintenance

Keep the rods clean, check the selector's full travel across all three Signature positions, and test all three tunes after any service, because a selector adjusted for one tune can drift off another. Never force the selector lever.

Build and restoration guidance

When setting a triple-Signature barrel, mark the third track before removing the barrel, verify the first quarter before the longer quarters, and record the selector positions in the service notes.

Tools

Chime rod gauges, selector tool, screwdrivers, and a tune chart.

title: Signature Full Hour Sequence
body:
Specifications

An original Signature full hour sequence that plays the Signature four-note tune in full at the top of the hour, followed by the hour strikes, in the same structure as the historical full hour sequence but with Signature notes. It is labelled signature-original and is never presented as Big Ben.

Mechanism

At the hour the clock plays the full Signature sequence, sixteen notes, and then strikes the hour, one strike for one o'clock up to twelve at twelve. The hour strike train is separate from the chime train, and the two are synchronised so the strike begins only after the last chime note, by the chime train's locking and the strike train's warning.

Maintenance

Keep the hour strike hammer and the chime hammers aligned, and check that the strike does not begin early. Test the full hour at least once after any service, not just the quarters, because the synchronisation fault shows only at the hour.

Build and restoration guidance

When synchronising, set the chime train to finish before the strike train's warning releases, and count the hour strikes at three different hours. Adjust the rack or count wheel, never the hands, to correct a wrong count.

Tools

Hammer alignment tool, screwdrivers, and a counting reference.

title: Signature Passing Strike
body:
Specifications

An original Signature passing strike that sounds a single blow as the hands pass the hour, without a full striking train, made for a Signature clock that needs an hour sound but not a counting strike. It is labelled signature-original and uses a tripping pin on the going train.

Mechanism

As the minute hand passes twelve, the pin trips a hammer that strikes a single rod once. The clock does not count the hours, so the passing strike marks that an hour has passed, not which hour it is. Its simplicity is its advantage: there is no strike train to synchronise and no rack or count wheel to wear.

Maintenance

Keep the tripping pin clean and the hammer pivot oiled, and check that the strike sounds exactly at the hour. A late passing strike usually has a bent pin or a loose hammer.

Build and restoration guidance

When fitting, set the pin so the hammer falls exactly as the minute hand reaches twelve, and test at several hours, because a pin set for one hour may drift if the going train has shake. Do not add a counting mechanism to a passing strike without adding a separate train.

Tools

Small files, hammer pivot oil, screwdrivers, and a timing reference.

title: Signature Full Hour Strike
body:
Specifications

An original Signature full hour strike that counts the hours on a dedicated striking train, with a warning step before the hour and a locking step after the last blow. It is labelled signature-original and is built on the standard warning-and-let-off structure with Signature lever shapes.

Mechanism

Before the hour the train is warned, the train runs a short way until it is caught, and at the hour the warning is released and the train strikes the correct number of blows, from one to twelve, then locks again. The warning step lets the first blow fall promptly on the hour, and the locking step stops the train cleanly after the last blow.

Maintenance

Keep the strike train pivots oiled and the warning lever clean, and check the strike count at every hour after a service. A strike that runs on past the hour usually has a worn locking face.

Build and restoration guidance

When restoring, set the warning firmly, set the locking cleanly, and test all twelve hours in order. Never adjust the hands to correct a wrong count; correct the rack or count wheel.

Tools

Strike train oil, warning lever gauge, screwdrivers, and a counting chart.

title: Signature Count-Wheel Striking
body:
Specifications

An original Signature count-wheel striking design with a wheel carrying notches of increasing depth, made for a Signature longcase clock that teaches the older striking system. It is labelled signature-original, and its wheel is cut with the standard 78-blow cycle.

Mechanism

The count wheel turns a little at each strike, and its notches let the locking lever drop in after the correct number of blows. Because the wheel must complete a full cycle of 78 blows before it repeats, the wheel and the hands must stay in step, and if they fall out of step the clock strikes the wrong hour until the wheel is turned back into agreement.

Maintenance

Keep the notches clean and the locking lever pivot oiled, and check the wheel's position after any hand adjustment. A Signature count-wheel clock that strikes one hour out after the hands were moved has fallen out of step, and the correction is to let it strike until it agrees again.

Build and restoration guidance

When restoring, check every notch for wear, set the locking lever to drop squarely into the notches, and test the full 78-blow cycle, not just one hour, before closing the movement.

Tools

Count-wheel gauge, locking lever tool, clock oil, and a 78-blow chart.

title: Signature Rack-and-Snail Striking
body:
Specifications

An original Signature rack-and-snail striking design with a snail cam on the hour wheel and a rack whose fall sets the blow count, made for a Signature longcase clock. It is labelled signature-original, and its snail steps are cut for the twelve hours.

Mechanism

As the hour approaches the rack is lifted and the snail turns with the hour wheel. At the hour the rack falls onto the snail's step for that hour, the strike train runs, gathering the rack one tooth per blow, until the rack is fully gathered and the train locks. Because the snail is driven by the hands, moving the hands forward resets the strike count automatically, so this design cannot strike out of step the way a count-wheel design can.

Maintenance

Keep the rack teeth and snail steps clean, oil the rack pivot lightly, and check that the rack falls fully onto the snail at every hour. A rack that hangs up strikes too few blows, usually because of dirt on the snail or a bent rack tooth.

Build and restoration guidance

When restoring, check the snail steps for wear, set the gathering pallet to take one tooth per blow, and test all twelve hours after any rack work.

Tools

Rack gauge, snail step gauge, clock oil, and a counting chart.

title: Signature Quarter Train
body:
Specifications

An original Signature quarter-hour striking train that plays the Signature quarter tunes, distinct from the hour strike train and the going train, and driven by its own weight so the chimes do not drain the going train. It is labelled signature-original.

Mechanism

The going train trips the quarter train at each quarter, the train runs through its warning and plays the barrel sequence for that quarter, and it locks again until the next quarter. The barrel turns once per hour, playing a longer part of its pinned sequence at each quarter, and the locking must be firm, or the train will overrun into the next quarter.

Maintenance

Keep the quarter train pivots oiled and the locking lever clean, and check that the train locks immediately after the last note of each quarter. A train that plays on usually has a worn locking face or a weak locking spring.

Build and restoration guidance

When restoring, set the warning, the barrel position, and the locking as a set, and test all four quarters in order, twice, before closing the movement.

Tools

Quarter train oil, locking lever tool, screwdrivers, and a quarter chart.

title: Signature Ting-Tang Strike
body:
Specifications

An original Signature ting-tang strike using two rods of different pitch, struck alternately for the hour count, made for a Signature clock where a single rod would be too plain. It is labelled signature-original.

Mechanism

At the hour the strike train drives two hammers alternately, high then low, for as many pairs as the hour requires, with a single extra blow on odd hours. The alternating action needs two hammer levers timed to alternate, which is more complex than a single-rod strike but simpler than a chime barrel.

Maintenance

Keep both rods clean and both hammers aligned, because a hammer striking off-centre on one rod makes the alternation sound uneven. Check the hammer timing after any service, since one hammer running late breaks the rhythm.

Build and restoration guidance

When restoring, set the two hammers to alternate evenly, check that each hammer lifts clear after its blow, and test at an odd hour and an even hour, because the odd hour's final single blow is where timing faults show.

Tools

Two-rod gauge, hammer alignment tool, clock oil, and screwdrivers.

title: Signature Song Chime
body:
Specifications

An original Signature song-like chime played on six rods, with a short invented melody rather than a permutation, made for a Signature clock whose owner wants a song-like quarter chime. It is labelled signature-original and is never presented as a historical melody.

Mechanism

The chime plays a short melodic phrase at each quarter, accumulating through the hour, so the half hour plays more of the melody than the first quarter, and the full hour plays the whole phrase followed by the hour strikes. Because the tune is melodic, its barrel is pinned as a melody, and the rods must be tuned to the melody's scale.

Maintenance

Keep the six rods clean and tuned, check the hammers in melodic order, and test the full hour after any service, since the melody's end is where faults show. Record the rod tuning in the service notes.

Build and restoration guidance

When setting the barrel, verify the melody's first phrase before the longer quarters, and confirm the hour strike follows the full phrase. Never file a rod to change a note without recording the change.

Tools

Chime rod gauges, hammer tool, screwdrivers, and a melody chart.

title: Signature Named-Day Chime
body:
Specifications

An original Signature chime named for a Signature feast day in the system's own calendar, played on the same multi-rod set as the other Signature chimes, and offered as a further chime option. It is labelled signature-original and uses its own invented sequence.

Mechanism

The sequence accumulates through the hour like the other quarter chimes, with a short sequence at the first quarter and the full sequence at the hour, followed by the hour strikes. The barrel carries the tune on its own track, and the selector moves the hammers or barrel to that track. The movement's own Signature chime chart is the authority for the exact notes.

Maintenance

Keep the rods clean, check the selector's full travel, and test all chime options after any service. A clock playing the wrong tune at one quarter usually has a selector or barrel-position fault.

Build and restoration guidance

When setting a multi-chime barrel, mark the track before removing the barrel, verify the first quarter before the longer quarters, and never force the selector lever.

Tools

Chime rod gauges, selector tool, screwdrivers, and the Signature chime chart.

title: Signature Musical Barrel
body:
Specifications

An original Signature musical barrel that plays an invented melody on the hour, with pins on a cylinder lifting levers that trip hammers onto rods. It is labelled signature-original, and its melody is a Signature composition, not a historical tune.

Mechanism

Pins on the barrel lift levers as the barrel turns, each lever trips a hammer onto a rod, and the melody is stored as pin positions. The barrel is driven by its own spring, governed so it turns at a steady speed, and the tune's tempo depends on the governor, not on the going train. Changing the tune means changing the barrel.

Maintenance

Keep the barrel pins clean and straight, oil the barrel pivots lightly, and check the governor, because a slow governor makes the tune drag and a fast one makes it rush. A tune that rushes at the end usually has a weakening governor spring.

Build and restoration guidance

When restoring, check every pin for tightness, replace missing pins with new ones of the same height, and test the tune at full wind and low wind. Never file a pin to change a note; move or replace it.

Tools

Barrel pin gauges, governor tool, clock oil, and a melody chart.

title: Signature Warning and Let-Off
body:
Specifications

An original Signature warning and let-off design that prepares the strike train before the hour and releases it exactly at the hour, built with Signature lever shapes. It is labelled signature-original.

Mechanism

A few minutes before the hour the going train lifts the warning lever, the strike train runs a short way until its locking lever catches it, and the train waits, warned. At the hour the going train trips the let-off, the locking lever releases, and the train runs through its full strike. If warning fails the strike lags, and if let-off fails the strike does not sound or sounds at the wrong time.

Maintenance

Keep the warning and let-off levers clean and their pivots oiled, and check the warning a few minutes before the hour, not just the strike at the hour. A lagging strike usually has a warning lever that lifts late or a let-off that sticks.

Build and restoration guidance

When restoring, set the warning to engage firmly before the hour, set the let-off to release cleanly at the hour, and test the warning at every hour, because a warning that works at three may fail at twelve if the cam is worn.

Tools

Warning lever gauge, let-off tool, clock oil, and screwdrivers.

title: Signature Grand Sonnerie
body:
Specifications

An original Signature grand sonnerie mode in which the clock chimes the quarters and then strikes the full hour count after every quarter, not only at the top of the hour. It is labelled signature-original and uses Signature sequencing levers.

Mechanism

At the first quarter it plays the quarter chime and then strikes one, at the half hour it plays the half-hour chime and then strikes the hour count, and so on, so the listener always hears both the quarter and the hour. The strike train is triggered by the chime train's completion, not directly by the going train, and the whole sequence takes longer than a simple quarter chime. Signature petite sonnerie, by contrast, strikes the hour only at the top of the hour.

Maintenance

Keep both trains oiled and synchronised, and check the sequence at every quarter after a service, because a clock that strikes before the chime finishes has a sequencing fault. Test at the first quarter as well as the hour, since the first quarter is where the hour strike after a quarter is most likely to be missed.

Build and restoration guidance

When restoring, set the chime train to complete and lock before the strike train is released, and test all four quarters in order, counting both the chime notes and the hour strikes at each. Never shorten the sequence to cure a fault; find the sequencing lever that is out of adjustment.

Tools

Sequencing lever gauge, clock oil, screwdrivers, and a quarter-and-hour chart.
